nameStory: The "freckled pelt" name comes from the distinctive dark green spots scattered across its surface, which look just like freckles on skin. These "freckles" are actually special structures called cephalodia that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria, making this lichen a tiny biological factory. The "pelt" part refers to its leather-like texture and how it lies flat against surfaces like an animal hide.
description: Freckled pelt lichen is one of New England's most impressive leafy lichens, forming large gray-green patches that can spread over a foot wide. Its most distinctive feature is the collection of small, dark green "freckles" scattered across its surface like spots on a dalmatian. When wet, the whole lichen turns a vibrant green color, but it fades to pale gray as it dries out. This substantial lichen grows in broad, overlapping lobes that feel somewhat like thick, damp felt when moist.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic dark green "freckles" (cephalodia) scattered across the surface like spots on a dog - these are the key identifying feature that gives this lichen its name

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when wet, fading to pale gray or whitish when dry - the color change is dramatic and happens as moisture levels change

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Large, leafy lobes that overlap like shingles, with individual lobes reaching 4 inches long and feeling thick and substantial, not papery

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: One of the larger lichens you'll encounter, often forming patches over a foot wide that are easily visible from several feet away

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on soil, moss, or decaying organic matter in moist areas, rarely on rock or bark like many other lichens

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Large, brown, disk-like apothecia (fruiting bodies) may appear on the lobe edges, looking like small buttons or saucers

habitat: Look for freckled pelt lichen in New England's cool, moist environments, particularly in higher elevation areas of the White Mountains and Green Mountains. It thrives on moss-covered soil, rotting logs, and organic-rich ground in coniferous and mixed forests where humidity stays high. You'll often find it in the same spots where you might see other moisture-loving plants like ferns and mosses.

seasonality.spring: As snow melts and moisture increases, the lichen transforms from pale gray to vibrant green, making the dark freckles especially prominent. This is an excellent time to spot its dramatic color changes.
seasonality.summer: During humid periods, it maintains its green coloration, but may fade to gray during dry spells. Look for the large brown fruiting bodies that often develop in summer.
seasonality.fall: Increased rainfall brings out the green coloration again, and the lichen may appear particularly lush against autumn's fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Visible under snow, appearing pale gray to whitish, but the distinctive freckled pattern remains the best identification feature even when dormant.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a triple partnership - it contains not just one but two different photosynthetic partners (a green alga and a blue-green bacteria), making it one of nature's most complex collaborative organisms that can both make its own food AND fix nitrogen from the air.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with dog pelt lichen, but dog pelt lacks the distinctive dark green freckles and has a different texture. Remember: "freckles = freckled pelt" - if you see those dark spots, you've found your lichen!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "green dog lichen" in some guides, "freckled pelt" is the preferred common name to avoid confusion with the more common dog pelt lichen. The scientific name "aphthosa" means "with thrush" or "ulcerated," referring to the spotted appearance that early botanists thought resembled mouth sores.
compareHints: Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward. Dog pelt lichen is similar in size and shape but lacks these spots and has a more uniform surface texture. Scaly pelt lichen has a distinctly scaly, rough texture rather than the smooth, freckled surface of freckled pelt.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
